different  the new version failed slightly more often

Poisson Trace · fix check · humaneval-a (old) and humaneval-b (new)

Summary

- Compared: old humaneval-a against new humaneval-b, on the same 328 inputs:
  10,496 tries of each. A try counts as failed when DeepEval marked its Tests
  Passed metric as not passed.
- Question: Did the new version fail more or less often than the old? You asked
  that the run be able to catch a 10-point drop in how often it fails.
- Answer: Slightly more failures, if tries of an input count as independent
  (here they are much alike). The new version failed 1,387 of 10,496 tries and
  the old 1,338 of 10,496 (0.47 more per 100 tries; the 10 points you set was
  for a drop, not a rise); 32 of the net 49 extra failures come from case
  HumanEval/129@0.7 and case HumanEval/129@0.0.
- Next: Run both versions side by side on these inputs with your own harness,
  then run `poisson-trace fix-check` on the two new runs.

Before you act on this

- Trace can't tell when they ran (the starts of humaneval-a and humaneval-b are
  when their files were written or copied), so it can't tell whether they were
  run side by side either: anything else that changed between them (the
  provider, the model behind the API, the day) may be part of the difference, in
  either direction.
- Both runs name the same target (import/deepeval); Trace can't tell what
  differs between them, only what you tell it.
- These results fit anything from 0.04 to 0.93 more failures per 100 tries
  (ranges built this way hold the true difference about 95 times in 100, if
  tries are independent), which does not include a 10-point drop.
- Tries of the same input are counted as separate chances; here they are much
  alike (agreement 0.78, where 0 is no more alike than chance and 1 is
  identical), and if they are near copies the answer is more confident than it
  should be.
- If each input failed equally often under both versions, a gap at least this
  big, either way, would turn up about 4 times in 100 (counting tries as
  independent).
- A check of which inputs went up and which went down can't rule out chance on
  its own (p = 0.127 in the report), so the gap rests on case HumanEval/129@0.7
  and case HumanEval/129@0.0. Without case HumanEval/129@0.7 and case
  HumanEval/129@0.0, the gap is 0.16 points (p = 0.47).
- The whole range is at most 0.93 points, under the 10 points you set (you set
  it for a drop; this is a rise), if tries of an input are independent.
- Before putting the difference down to the version, run both side by side.

The two versions

The old version and the new on the same inputs.

version    runs  failed  failure share  did not fail

old      10,496   1,338          12.7%         87.3%
new      10,496   1,387          13.2%         86.8%

The old version did not fail on 87.3% of its episodes on these inputs.

The comparison

exact conditional Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test, stratified by input over 328
  inputs (58 informative), two-sided; α = 0.05.

new failures: observed 1,387, expected 1,362.500, variance 131.139; p = 0.036
difference: +0.47 points, new minus old (+0.04 to +0.93; Mantel-Haenszel
  weights; range: stratified Miettinen-Nurminen score interval, 95%, for these
  inputs as run)
by input: p = 0.127 (sign-flip over the 47 inputs that moved, 100,000 draws,
  seed = 0); not part of the line below

Consistency

failure share 0.130 · fails again 0.808 · κ 0.779 · within-input variance 0.025
  against pooled 0.113
a comparison that ignored the inputs would need 1/(1 − κ) = 4.52 times the runs

What it could not have detected

proportional change on every input, 80% power, α = 0.05, continuity-corrected
  normal approximation to the stratified statistic.

- a drop in failure share: could not have detected one below 0.64 points
- a rise in failure share: could not have detected one below 0.66 points

different: the new version failed more on these inputs (exact
  Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel, stratified by input, p = 0.036)

10 of 328 inputs shown, by ascending p; --json lists all.

A lone changed input is flagged only if its p is below α / M = 0.000152, and the
  smallest p an input of this design can give is 1.09e-18: a lone change can be
  flagged; a lone complete flip needs 9 repeats per arm. An input with no flag
  is not an input that did not change.

- wall_time_s: too small to tell: the test is quiet (p = 0.239; a call needs p
  below 0.05), and changes smaller than about ±0.00000786 s (2.2%) could easily
  go unseen in a run like this. In words, these results fit anything from
  0.00000188 s faster to 0.00000811 s slower. To decide, choose how much change
  would not matter before you look, as a share of the old mean: --max-change
  wall_time_s=X%. For the typical case (Hodges-Lehmann estimate) the change is
  -0.000000282 s (95% range -0.00000203 s to +0.00000163 s). Over 328 paired
  cases: old mean 0.000354 s, new mean 0.000357 s (change +0.00000312 s,
  +0.88%); middle case (P50) 0.000351 s old, 0.00035 s new; P90 0.00037 s old,
  0.000372 s new.
- input_chars: identical on all 328 cases; a change touching more than about 3
  in 328 cases like these would usually have shown up.
- output_chars: too small to tell: the test is quiet (p = 0.145; a call needs p
  below 0.025), and changes smaller than about ±0.0923 chars (1.3%) could easily
  go unseen in a run like this. In words, these results fit anything from 0.0146
  chars shorter to 0.103 chars longer. To decide, choose how much change would
  not matter before you look, as a share of the old mean: --max-change
  output_chars=X%. For the typical case (Hodges-Lehmann estimate) the change is
  0 chars (95% range 0 chars to 0 chars). Over 328 paired cases: old mean 7.27
  chars, new mean 7.31 chars (change +0.0441 chars, +0.61%); middle case (P50) 6
  chars old, 6 chars new; P90 12.4 chars old, 13.8 chars new.

What this cannot say

- A difference between two stored runs is a difference between the runs. The
  version, the provider and the hour changed together unless the two were run
  side by side, and this test cannot separate them.
- Repeat runs of one input are read as separate draws and never as replays: a
  served model is not bit-identical on repeat, so nothing here matches a run of
  the old version to a run of the new by seed.
- If repeat runs of one input are near copies of one another, the run-level test
  overstates its confidence. The by-input line does not depend on that.
- Rows with no outcome are left out of both arms and counted in the header. A
  new version that times out where the old one failed does not show as a failure
  here.
- Trace reads the runs it is given. If the inputs were chosen by the old arm's
  own outcomes, or the more favourable of several runs was handed over, the
  confidence printed does not hold.
- The detection limit and the run counts are computed from these runs' own
  failure rates, which are estimates. They are a guide to the next design, not a
  promise about it.
